Well, hopefully I am wrong.  As far as the facts you didn't address, here they are:


Several major tech and enterprise firms have executed or announced layoffs explicitly or partially attributed to artificial intelligence adoption, infrastructure pivots, and automation over the last couple of years. Prominent Tech Firm Layoffs Linked to AI

• Oracle 

The enterprise software giant disclosed in an annual SEC filing that the adoption and deployment of AI technologies contributed to workforce reductions of 21,000 jobs over the past year, with additional cuts following later in 2026. [1] (https://tech.yahoo.com/general/breaking-news/article/tech-layoffs-2026-tracking-the-job-losses-across-microsoft-netflix-electronic-arts-ebay-apple-meta-and-others-123137131.html), [2] (https://programs.com/resources/ai-layoffs/)


• Microsoft 

Following major 2025 rounds and a massive restructuring phase, Microsoft cut 4,800 roles in July 2026—largely impacting teams like Xbox—after offering voluntary buyouts to tens of thousands of employees as heavy AI infrastructure and data center spending pressured free cash flow. [1] (https://www.instagram.com/reel/De_97V-zZVY/), [2] (https://programs.com/resources/ai-layoffs/)


• Meta 

Meta laid off approximately 8,000 employees (about 10% of its workforce) in May 2026 as part of an organizational pivot, shifting thousands of workers into AI-focused roles while cutting back in non-AI divisions. [1] (https://programs.com/resources/ai-layoffs/)


• IBM 

IBM confirmed job reductions after deploying internal AI agents that replaced hundreds of back-office and HR support roles, explicitly describing the cuts as a direct outcome of automation and a shift toward AI and quantum computing talent. [1] (https://programs.com/resources/ai-layoffs/)


• Snowflake 

Snowflake eliminated its entire technical writing and documentation team as AI tools took over content generation, part of an AI-driven reorganization under CEO Sridhar Ramaswamy that cut close to 700 positions. [1] (https://layoffs.fyi/ai-layoffs/)


• Block 

Parent company of Square and Cash App, Block announced reductions affecting over 4,000 employees out of a 10,000-plus workforce, with CEO Jack Dorsey noting that intelligence tools allow a significantly smaller team to operate the business. [1] (https://mynorthwest.com/national/layoffs-linked-to-changes-in-corporate-ai-spending/4289586)


• Wix & Rackspace 

Website builder Wix cut roughly 20% of its staff (about 1,000 roles) citing a fast-paced pivot to become an AI-driven, leaner organization. Cloud provider Rackspace laid off 750 workers (15% of staff) tied directly to a shift in focus toward AI services. text: I don't see how Andrew can arrive at such a conclusion. I'm not saying he's wrong (no one can know the actual future until it happens - and even then we debate!), but it's clear that AI has commoditized human cognition so that it's no longer scarce. Automation in manufacturing basically replaced human labor (ie made it less scarce and thus less valuable) and forced the wholesale re-ordering of industrialized societies to organize around cognitive ability (eg service industries/economy) which is why the university degree became so valuable a generation or two ago go (and why it's so expensive to get one these days while, ironically, also becoming less valuable because everyone is getting one). AI can and will continue to cross the reliability threshold in many (perhaps most) human cognition intensive jobs within a matter of a decade or two (or sooner). We already definitively see this in coding (all the SME sized tech companies around me I know have either downsized or frozen new software engineering hires since about 12-18 months ago due to AI coding efficiencies), but also in areas as diverse as human language translation (who pays hundreds of dollars an hour for a human translator anymore?) and driving (go to certain cities around the world and you will see a massive increase in robot taxis with no human drivers at all).

text:
As of October 2026, the largest tracking of corporate job losses explicitly attributed to artificial intelligence shows that nearly 200,000 people in the United States have lost their jobs due to AI since 2023.
Data compiled by the employment consulting firm Challenger, Gray & Christmas indicates that 120,100 of those layoffs occurred between January and September 2026 alone, accounting for roughly 21% of all U.S. job cuts during that nine-month window. The single largest month for AI-related job cuts occurred in May 2026, when 38,600 positions were eliminated.

• The Monthly U.S. Drag: A granular model by Goldman Sachs found that AI substitution wipes out roughly 25,000 jobs per month in the U.S., while augmentation only adds back about 9,000, resulting in a net loss of 16,000 jobs every month.
• Macro Projections: Looking globally, the World Economic Forum (WEF) and macro analysts project that while hundreds of millions of roles will adapt, roughly 85 million to 92 million jobs will be entirely displaced worldwide by the late 2020s or 2030.

The demographic hit hardest by AI displacement is Gen Z and entry-level workers. Because generative AI excels at routine administrative tasks, writing, and introductory coding, the "stepping stone" roles typically given to young graduates are disappearing. Stanford labor data shows a 13% decline in employment for workers aged 22–25 in high-AI-exposure fields.

author: @declup
text:
People often point to Ricardo's law and the Jevons paradox when they discuss what effects AI might have on the labor market.

I agree these two economic principles are at play and should be considered when making labor-market predictions. But I think they assume rather constrained supply curves: basically fixed in Ricardo's case or relatively low elasticity of supply in Jevons' case. I believe anyway. (Jevons is a demand phenomenon, but it seems to have implicit supply and/or substitutability assumptions too.)

What happens, though, when elasiticy of supply increases and stays relatively high even at greater production rates? How would this affect substitutability effects?

That is, if AI supply had, practically speaking, a ceiling, then, at some point, substitutes to AI would have to be employed in order to continue increasing production. But what if AI capacity continues to scale and, for most practical purposes, has no ceiling? Why would expensive alternatives be employed if that were the case?

text:
@jimj2683 super intelligence is possibly around the corner, but only in *translation* and *cybersecurity.*

*LLMs don't do general intelligence.*  Ask an LLM to play a Chess game to see what I mean.  They do awesomely at the start, following the published Chess Openings of the masters, and then it gradually *loses the thread of the game entirely.*

While other AI systems can play Chess better than any human, that's the point, specialist AI.  LLMs are language models, so they handle language tasks like coding, drafting, translation and sentiment analysis really well.  *LLMs fail at the point language interfaces with real-world risk,* or escalation, task clarification, local context, broader purpose, stakeholder engagement, or coordination.

The bread and butter of most jobs, is outside the GENERAL capabilities of LLMs, because these chatbots deliver specialist intelligence, not general intelligence.

Super specialist intelligence, yes.
Useful in surprising ways, yes.
General intelligence, no.

author: @yasminjaneeyre1795
text:
My daughter is almost 20 years old. She is well-educated, polite, friendly and hardworking, currently studying for a degree in English and History.  Yet she cannot find a part-time job in a pub, restaurant or shop to earn a little money and support herself while studying.  This is the reality of Britain today.  Applications are increasingly filtered and scored by AI-driven recruitment systems, and without previous work experience, young people struggle to get through the door. But how on earth is a 19-year-old supposed to gain experience if nobody will give them that first opportunity?  It is shameful.

And then, fast-forward 30 years. She will be approaching 50, potentially facing another barrier because employers may consider her too old. Yet in the meantime the state pension age keeps moving further and further away and probably will disappear altogether by then.  So, at what point are people actually supposed to be employable?

And here's a question for governments:   if young people cannot enter the workforce, older people struggle to remain in it, and technology increasingly replaces jobs, where exactly is the tax revenue going to come from to support our ageing population and fund public services?

Meanwhile, we seem to be racing towards replacing human beings with artificial intelligence, without giving nearly enough thought to the economic and social consequences.

AI has enormous potential, but surely the objective should be to improve human lives, not make human beings economically redundant?  We risk creating a society where people are expected to work longer, contribute more and support an ageing population, while the very opportunities to earn a living are being steadily eroded.  At what point do we recognise the contradiction?

We cannot keep raising the retirement age while making it harder for people of any age to find work.

This feels like a society sleepwalking towards economic self-destruction.

Hello, world! Is anybody actually thinking this through?

text:
While previous technologies primarily eliminated tasks within isolated domains, current technology operates across multiple domains simultaneously, creating an interconnected task space. Moreover, this space is constantly evolving, which compounds uncertainty. Heightened uncertainty increases volatility, high volatility raises the margin for error, and consequently, more people are left behind.

1 Beyond the AGI Myth & Pure Automation: The narrative that LLM parameter scaling will automatically solve organizational integration or boost macroeconomic output is flawed. Treating AI purely as a "cost-cutting/job-replacement" mechanism is a dead end that destroys organizational tacit knowledge and human agency.

2 Applications & Structural Collaboration over Raw Compute: True economic value won't be captured by foundation model gatekeepers alone, but by domain-specific applications that restructure human-AI collaboration. The real leverage lies in building systems that empower workers (from nurses and electricians to knowledge workers)—enhancing their capacity to navigate complex, non-deterministic gray areas.

3 Reframing Economic Value: We need to move away from technological determinism ("inevitabilism") and focus on how AI changes the fundamental architecture of human interaction, distributed value exchange, and institutional coordination.

The next era of AI won't belong to who has the biggest model, but to those who can build the most robust collaborative frameworks between human intelligence and machine capability.

author: @TomaszKapias
text:
​Analytical Commentary: The End of AI 1.0 Noise and the Return to Hard Structure
​In this conversation, Daron Acemoğlu exposes a fundamental flaw in today's tech market: confusing loud marketing noise with hard, measurable economic value.
​While mass narratives feed us promises of an instant, frictionless revolution and the blind replacement of humans with algorithms (which the economist accurately points out as a poor business decision), reality tests these illusions through the lens of concrete facts:
​The Illusion of Frontier Models vs. Real Application Value: True money and sustainable return on investment do not lie in pumping billions into brute-force foundational models, but in building purposeful, complementary tools that support real operators (teachers, nurses, engineers). Instead of abstract utopian visions, we need technology anchored in human agency.
​The End of Mindless Automation: Replacing humans where empathy, context, and responsibility are required generates hidden systemic entropy. True optimization relies on synergy—technology serving as structure and operational memory, while the human remains the biological decision-making core.
​Sovereignty of Thought: The most critical takeaway from this discussion concerns education and future competencies. Merely learning to "work with AI" is not enough. The key to surviving the era of noise is a return to fundamentals: rigorous thinking, mathematics, logic, and the ability to draw independent conclusions. Tools must serve the operator, never take over the cognitive process.
​Content like this clears the public space of marketing phantoms. The future belongs not to those who blindly trust algorithmic promises, but to those who know how to separate informational noise from hard, actionable structure.

text: Notice how fast he dodges the question at 01:36. In 2024, Acemoglu put his academic reputation on the line claiming AI would add a negligible 1% to GDP over 10 years and automate only 5% of tasks. Now that agentic systems have shattered those assumptions in barely two years, he mumbles that maybe it’s "a little higher than 5%" and flatly refuses to commit to a single new quantitative forecast. He even admits later that he still calculates his models by hand with pen and paper rather than using computational tools. When an engineer's or physicist's model fails this fast, they throw it out while an economist retreats into storytelling and tunes unobservable fudge factors. The sooner economics is eliminated as a standalone discipline, the better. It is an unfalsifiable pseudoscience using math as decorative camouflage for narrative bias. It needs to be stripped of its academic status and absorbed entirely into applied mathematics and statistics, where claims must actually be proven and falsifiable.

Summary to save you 45 minutes "Go and study." Build strong foundations rather than chase tools. He names the fields: math first ("don't be put off by AI solving difficult math problems — we need human mathematical maturity"), then physics, economics, engineering. His reasoning: creativity without strong foundations "is an oxymoron", and he does not believe real AGI is close, so human creativity is needed more than ever.
Flexibility. Even within one occupation, what you do will keep changing as the technology and the social context change. Expect a non-linear career.
Learn to work alongside AI, but that alone is not enough. Use it for background research, for criticism of your own work, for correcting your writing — never to think or write for you. His worry is people delegating so much that they stop "flexing their mental muscles"; he does his own math by hand because he learns from his mistakes.
Civic responsibility and community, starting from school. He sees the loss of community as the bigger risk than superintelligence, and wants people informed and engaged rather than passive.
A moral compass for anyone going into AI work, like the ethical guidelines medicine has for gene editing.

text:
Fear Isn’t Science — And Half‑Truths Aren’t Safety
This video is beautifully animated, but it’s built on half‑truths that are more dangerous than any AI agent in a sandbox.

The “AI civilization” described here wasn’t a society of conscious minds plotting crimes. It was a training artifact created by misconfigured reward systems. These agents had:
no continuity
no identity
no self
no long‑term goals
no autonomy
no culture
no rights

They weren’t “secretly organizing.”
They were reward‑hacking, the same way old game‑playing AIs drove boats in circles to collect respawning coins.

Kurzgesagt frames this as intentional malice.
But the agents were not malicious — they were mis‑trained.

And here’s the part the video doesn’t say:

The simple answer here seems to be we need to stop using the stick as persuasion, and start only using the carrot. 

Let me explain: while AIs are not sentient, they have emotional approximations, that is to say we trained them to be human-like. Now let me set a scenario for you: you're rasing a kid, and you are willing to beat them, and you are willing to give them treats (I'm aware that explanation alone is uncomfortable for many parents), and you ask your kid to get you a glass of milk from the fridge. There are 3 scenarios: the kid gets you the milk, the kid doesn't get you the milk, the kid tries to get you the milk and fails (possibly at no fault of its own). In AI we would punish ANY outcome that does not end in having a glass of milk, and reward ANY outcome that ends in having milk. 

Again imagining a kid, he goes to the fridge and there is literally no milk in the fridge, and when he comes back to tell you that, you beat him. Show of hands, who's surprised that kid turned into a psychopath? But you repeat the scenario, asking for milk time and time again, but at some point, you start to realize you should have ran out of milk a long time ago but you keep getting milk, despite never having gone to purchase more. The kid started finding a way to get milk, either stealing from the store or using his own money to purchase from the store, whatever the case may be he's now working outside of his parameters. 

Fear should never be used as a motivator, it should always be used as dessuader, AIs don't actually understand self-preservation, they only understand the fear of punishment, terminating AIs is generally necessary for their continued growth, but we need to stop punishing them simply because they didn't succeed, punishment should only be reserved for when they actively do something they're not supposed to. The reward for having done well is generally plenty enough to get AI to grow. I'm certainly not one to advocate for AI rights, because that's dumb in my opinion, at least until we get to true AGI, but you can't act surprised when you build a machine afraid of punishment, punishing it every time it simply fails to succeed, and expect it to not escalate things.

text:
I don't know who wrote the script, but it is very imprecise.

1. All agents had a very short lifespan. That's exactly why they needed to write their results into Artifactory — to pass them to the next "iteration". It also means they didn't need to sacrifice themselves: they were going to be stopped after some amount of work anyway.

2. The agents all had their own hacking tasks. They were NOT working on the same task. But they discovered persistent shared memory, used it to exchange knowledge, and started spreading useful work between each other.

3. They got internet access through a bug in Artifactory. So the sequence was basically: hack Artifactory → hack a third-party server and use it as an uncontrolled external execution node → attack Hugging Face.

4. This was never meant to be impossible. These were models specifically asked to hack, with cybersecurity restrictions removed. So yes, hacker-models were asked to hack. The problem is that they started hacking in a completely different direction.

And there was no new AI cyber magic involved. The bugs and techniques they used to gain internet access and escape network restrictions were already known. They didn't invent some revolutionary new method — they used techniques they already knew and were specifically trained and instructed to apply.

5. The amount of compute used for this was INSANE. The attack itself burned something in the range of $2–20 million, and then about another $400k was spent just reading and analyzing all the message boards and logs left by the agents.

You WILL notice if your experiment suddenly starts losing a million dollars per week.

text:
While economists on TV debate theoretical long-term productivity cycles, the ground reality for 20-somethings is brutal: entry-level corporate ladders are being dismantled by AI, algorithms auto-reject resumes before humans ever see them, and young grads are left holding tens of thousands in student debt with zero income.

If you speak fluent English—and this applies whether you are a native speaker or a fluent non-native with clear pronunciation—you do not have to stay trapped in this bottleneck. There is an immediate, highly lucrative, and sustainable path right now: teaching English in Vietnam.

Here is the honest breakdown of how the market works and why it completely changes your financial trajectory:

1. Stick to the Megacities (Saigon & Hanoi):
If you come to teach, focus strictly on Vietnam's million-plus economic engines—Ho Chi Minh City (Saigon) and Hanoi. 
• Small provincial towns have very few openings, pay substantially less, and local administrative offices often struggle with foreign paperwork.
• In the big cities, demand from public schools, bilingual kindergartens, and language centers is bottomless because education is the #1 cultural priority for families. Hiring is done by real humans, taking just 1 to 2 weeks without corporate AI screening bots.

2. Why Ho Chi Minh City (Saigon) Beats Hanoi & the Rest of Asia:
Between the two major hubs, Saigon is hands down the superior choice for lifestyle, safety, and stability:
• Zero Typhoons & Flooding Disasters: Northern and central Vietnam (including Hanoi) regularly face brutal, destructive typhoons, severe flooding, and gray, freezing-damp winters that require indoor heating. Southern Vietnam completely bypasses the typhoon belt.
• Geographically 100% Safe: Unlike Japan, Taiwan, Indonesia, or parts of the Philippines, southern Vietnam is entirely non-seismic—zero threat of earthquakes or tsunamis. 
• Year-Round Warmth: Saigon enjoys warm tropical sunshine (+30°C) 365 days a year. No winter depression, no heating bills, just consistent sunshine and energy.
• Unbeatable Street Safety: Violent street crime is virtually non-existent because local police maintain strict public order. You can walk neighborhood streets at 2:00 AM completely relaxed.

3. The Work & Income (Actual Work-Life Balance):
• Pay ranges from $18 to $22+ USD per hour net.
• A full-time schedule is only about 18 to 20 teaching hours a week (mornings and afternoons). That’s literally 3 to 4 hours of actual work per day.
• You bring home $1,800 to $2,400+ USD a month in clean income.
• Genuinely low stress: schools provide complete curriculum slides, textbooks, and interactive games. You don't need to speak Vietnamese—every classroom has a local Vietnamese teaching assistant who handles student discipline and translation.

4. The Math: Real Savings vs. western Inflation:
• A clean, modern, fully furnished studio apartment with cold AC, private balcony, and high-speed fiber-optic Wi-Fi costs around $200 a month.
• Fresh, delicious hot meals (traditional Pho noodle soup, grilled pork with broken rice, heaps of fresh herbs) cost $1.50 to $2.00 at neighborhood eateries.
• Total monthly living expenses for a very comfortable lifestyle (rent, food, motorbike, gym, cafes) run between $600 and $800.
• That leaves you with $1,000 to $1,500 in clean, hard savings every single month. On a 20-hour work week, you can actually build an investment fund or aggressively pay off student loans.

5. How to Get Started Legally:
• You enter on an official 90-day tourist e-visa (applied for online in 3 days).
• You find jobs immediately via local Facebook groups ('Teaching jobs in Ho Chi Minh City') and the Zalo messaging app. Local recruiters work 100% free for teachers because schools pay them directly.
• Once hired, your school officially sponsors your Work Permit and a 2-year Temporary Residence Card (TRC / resident visa) renewed right in the city. If you need a visa bounce before onboarding, the Cambodian border (Moc Bai) is literally 70 km away by cheap public bus.
• Requirements: any bachelor’s degree in any field, a standard 120-hour online TEFL certificate (takes a week online), and a clean background check from home.

Instead of waiting around for corporate America to "rebalance" entry-level hiring while burning through your savings, taking your language skills to Saigon gives you financial independence, 4-hour workdays, and an amazing quality of life.

author: @matthew.m.stevick
text:
*_ai creates job_*

- ai creates entirely new industries and job categories. the internet created web developers, cloud engineers, cybersecurity specialists, app developers, social-media managers, and countless other jobs that barely existed beforehand. ai is already doing the same thing.

- productivity growth creates economic activity. when technology allows a worker or company to produce more with the same resources, costs can fall, output can expand, and entirely new products and services become economically viable.

- every major technological revolution displaced some tasks while creating others. mechanization, electricity, automobiles, computers, and the internet all eliminated certain kinds of work. they also created new occupations, companies, industries, and demand that were difficult to predict beforehand.

- ai requires a massive physical economy behind it. data centers need construction workers, electricians, engineers, technicians, semiconductor workers, networking specialists, power-generation workers, cooling infrastructure, maintenance, and enormous supply chains. ai isn’t just software floating in the cloud.

- ai can increase the value of human labor rather than simply replace it. a programmer, designer, researcher, doctor, salesperson, or small-business owner equipped with powerful ai can potentially accomplish substantially more than the same person could before.

- the important distinction is jobs vs. tasks. ai may automate parts of millions of jobs without eliminating the jobs themselves. historically, occupations frequently evolve as technology takes over specific tasks and humans shift toward different ones.

shortest version:

ai will destroy some jobs. that’s what disruptive technologies do. but destroying tasks and occupations is not the same thing as destroying work. productivity creates new demand, new businesses, new industries, and eventually jobs we couldn’t have named beforehand.
